why: Tested and not supported as written. The halves do cut few countries, but the slivers ARE parts of countries, so country totals cannot decide: with one map's totals held in blocks of 5, 10 or 30 degrees and the other map's pattern inside, the lead swings between 1.7 and 7.4 million (check/out/edge-2020.out). What the tests support is the narrower thing: the model's fine spreading hardly matters (blur over 0.55 degrees: -0.14, -0.08, -0.21 million on GHS-POP, newer and older WorldPop; one map's totals in 1-degree blocks with the other's pattern inside: -0.08, +0.12). Blur over 1.05 degrees: -2.04, -1.85, -1.98; over 2.05 degrees the lead becomes -1.63, -2.05, -3.85. People within 1 degree of the Berlin half's edge: 92.4, 90.3, 92.9 million; Manila is 90 km inside, Singapore 42 km, Rio de Janeiro 47 km (check/out/cities.out).

## 4. Under "How far to trust this", in the paragraph "None of the data is mine."

OLD:

> the population maps from the European Commission's Joint Research Centre,

NEW:

> the population maps from the European Commission's Joint Research Centre and, for the check of 26 November, from WorldPop (www.worldpop.org) at the University of Southampton,
why: The page will show a figure made from WorldPop's data and state results from it, and neither of its two credit passages names WorldPop. The note says the data are under CC BY 4.0, which requires the credit (the checker could not confirm the licence without the network). The credits "in full" at the foot are inside the part printed "as it stood until 25 November", so the story's own paragraph is the place. It is put here at the head of the file because no other text in the file can anchor it.

old: > Two other population maps, made by another group, tell the same story: the Alps in 2000 and 2010, near Berlin in 2020. One of them is built on the censuses taken around 2020, which the maps I first used are not.
new: > Two other series of population maps, made by another group, agree as far as they go. The older series has the centre in the Alps in 2000 and 2010 and near Berlin in 2020. The newer series begins in 2015 and has the centre near Berlin from then on; unlike the maps I first used, it knows the censuses taken around 2020. On all three the lead is thin: in 2020 the half centred near Berlin holds between 2.6 and 4.9 million more people than the half centred in the Alps, out of nearly 8,000 million.
why: As written, both maps "tell the same story: the Alps in 2000 and 2010", and the next sentence lets the reader think the map that knows the 2020 censuses is one of the tellers. It is not: the newer series has no map before 2015. The draft also puts the good news in the main text and every caution further down; a stranger who reads only this section should meet the thin margin here.

new: The newer series, by its makers' account, is built on the censuses of about 2010 and about 2020.
why: This rests on the release statement alone ("Population and boundary data were gathered for the two most-recent census rounds (c.2010 and c.2020)", with other sources where there was no census); the note says "by its own account" and the page should too.

old: So the move is seen on three maps. But the three are not independent: all of them spread census counts over the ground by a model, none gives a margin of error, and the lead of one half over the other in 2020 is between 3 and 5 million people out of nearly 8,000 million.
new: So three sets of maps agree on where the centre is in 2020. The move itself is seen on only two of them, the two that go back before 2015, and those two start from the same censuses of about 2010; the newer series, the only one that knows the censuses of about 2020, begins when the centre is already near Berlin. Nor are the three independent: all of them spread census counts over the ground by a model, the newer series starts its map of buildings from the one that the maps I first used are built on, none gives a margin of error, and the lead of one half over the other in 2020 is between 2.6 and 4.9 million people out of nearly 8,000 million. The edge of the half centred near Berlin passes within 100 km of Manila, Singapore and Rio de Janeiro, with all three just inside it.
why: "The move is seen on three maps" is not so: the newer WorldPop series starts in 2015 with the Berlin half already 3.2 million ahead, so it shows no move; the two that show one (GHS-POP and the older WorldPop series) share the censuses of about 2010, which is the very weakness this paragraph was written to confess. That caution is in the note and was left out here. "Between 3 and 5 million" is not true of 2.6. The last sentence (from the checker's own count: Manila 90 km, Singapore 42 km, Rio 47 km inside the edge) may be dropped without harm to the rest.

old: The line for the map this page used starts
new: The line for the maps this page first used starts
why: After the change the page uses three sets of maps, so "the map this page used" no longer picks one out. Goes with relabelling the figure (see the report).

old: Where a line crosses "level", the best centre passes from the Alps to near Berlin. The years in the grey band are projections.
new: Where a line crosses "level", the half centred near Berlin overtakes the half centred in the Alps. The best centre is found separately, by a search over the whole globe: on each set of maps it is in the Alps in every year below the level and near Berlin in every year above it, except that in 2015, on the maps this page first used, a place in Bavaria ties with it. The years in the grey band are projections, and so is the older WorldPop point for 2020: those maps were made in 2018. The whole scale is small: 5 million people is 0.06% of the world's.
why: The lines compare two fixed halves; the best centre is a separate search, and the caption stated as a rule what is only an observed coincidence at five- and ten-year steps (and not quite that for GHS-POP's 2015, where the line is above level and the Palatinate ties). The checker's own search confirms the coincidence for the other fourteen points. The grey band marks 2025 and 2030 only, but the older WorldPop series was made in 2018, so its 2020 is projected too. And a stranger looking at an axis that runs from 10 fewer to 10 more needs telling that the whole range is about a quarter of one percent of mankind.
